claim: More than three-quarters of UK doctoral students and early-career researchers experienced a negative impact of lockdown on their ability to collect data, discuss ideas and findings with colleagues, and disseminate research findings.
source: We found that more than three-quarters of respondents were experiencing a negative impact of the lockdown on their ability to collect data, discuss ideas and findings with colleagues, and disseminate research findings.
evidence: Based on survey data collected from respondents about lockdown impacts

claim: More than half of UK doctoral students and early-career researchers identified a negative impact of lockdown on data analysis, writing, and working on grant or fellowship applications.
source: More than half also identified a negative impact on data analysis, writing, and working on grant or fellowship applications.
evidence: Based on survey responses about specific research activities

claim: Almost a third of UK doctoral students and early-career researchers had reduced or no access to software needed for research during lockdown.
source: In addition, almost a third of respondents identified that they had reduced or no access to the software that they needed for research, highlighting the importance for universities to provide better access to essential work resources.
evidence: Based on survey data about access to research software

claim: Universities need to provide better access to essential work resources for doctoral students and early-career researchers.
source: In addition, almost a third of respondents identified that they had reduced or no access to the software that they needed for research, highlighting the importance for universities to provide better access to essential work resources.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that a third of respondents lacked software access

claim: Half of UK doctoral students and early-career researchers reported being very stressed about their work during lockdown.
source: This decreased ability to work is creating stress: half of respondents reported being very stressed about their work, and two-thirds are very worried about their future plans.
evidence: Based on survey responses about stress levels

claim: Two-thirds of UK doctoral students and early-career researchers are very worried about their future plans during lockdown.
source: This decreased ability to work is creating stress: half of respondents reported being very stressed about their work, and two-thirds are very worried about their future plans.
evidence: Based on survey responses about future concerns

claim: Only 12% of final-year doctoral students reported that their institution had provided an option to extend their studies during the pandemic.
source: Concern about the future is real: only 12% of final-year doctoral students reported that their institution had provided an option to extend their studies.
evidence: Based on survey data from final-year doctoral students

claim: UKRI funding provisions for additional support during the pandemic only support a minority of doctoral students.
source: While UKRI has made some provisions for additional funding, it supports only a minority of doctoral students.
evidence: Statement about the limited scope of UKRI funding support

claim: There is a general lack of certainty among doctoral students and early-career researchers about whether they will be allowed to extend their studies and whether funding will be available.
source: There is a general lack of certainty among this population about whether they will be allowed to extend their studies, and whether funding will be available to support them to do so.
evidence: Based on survey responses indicating uncertainty about extensions and funding

claim: 40% of research staff reported that their research contract ends during 2020.
source: Among research staff, 40% reported that their research contract ends during 2020, and only 10% of this group report that their funding has been extended in the context of the pandemic.
evidence: Based on survey data from research staff about contract end dates

claim: Only 10% of research staff whose contracts end in 2020 reported that their funding has been extended in the context of the pandemic.
source: Among research staff, 40% reported that their research contract ends during 2020, and only 10% of this group report that their funding has been extended in the context of the pandemic.
evidence: Based on survey data from research staff about funding extensions

claim: The pandemic and lockdown have highlighted the precarious employment position of many early-career researchers.
source: The pandemic and the resulting lockdown have highlighted the precarious employment position of many early-career researchers, and should encourage the sector to consider whether it is morally acceptable to continue the practice of short-term employment contracts.
evidence: Inferred from the data about contract endings and lack of extensions

claim: The academic sector should consider whether it is morally acceptable to continue the practice of short-term employment contracts for early-career researchers.
source: The pandemic and the resulting lockdown have highlighted the precarious employment position of many early-career researchers, and should encourage the sector to consider whether it is morally acceptable to continue the practice of short-term employment contracts.
evidence: Normative claim based on the observed precarious employment situation

claim: Three-quarters of UK doctoral students and early-career researchers showed low levels of mental wellbeing during lockdown.
source: Three-quarters of respondents showed low levels of mental wellbeing and four in five showed some level of mental distress.
evidence: Based on survey data measuring mental wellbeing

claim: Four in five UK doctoral students and early-career researchers showed some level of mental distress during lockdown.
source: Three-quarters of respondents showed low levels of mental wellbeing and four in five showed some level of mental distress.
evidence: Based on survey data measuring mental distress

claim: Individuals working in arts and humanities reported higher levels of mental distress and loneliness during lockdown compared to other disciplines.
source: Experiences are not equal, however: individuals working in arts and humanities reported higher levels of mental distress and loneliness.
evidence: Based on survey data comparing mental health outcomes across disciplines

claim: Researchers with a physical disability or long-term illness can find it challenging to work from home if they do not have access to assistive technology.
source: Researchers with a physical disability or long-term illness can also find it challenging to work from home if they do not have access to the assistive technology they require.
evidence: Based on survey responses or observations about accessibility challenges

claim: International researchers working in the UK are lonelier and more stressed about many aspects of day-to-day life, living arrangements, finances and work during lockdown.
source: Finally, international researchers working in the UK are lonelier and more stressed about many aspects of day-to-day life, living arrangements, finances and work.
evidence: Based on survey data comparing international and domestic researchers

claim: Researchers who are less likely to have strong social support networks within and beyond academia in the UK may be more likely to be struggling with their mental wellbeing during lockdown.
source: Overall, our data suggest that researchers who are less likely to have strong social support networks within and beyond academia in the UK may be more likely to be struggling with their mental wellbeing.
evidence: Inferred from survey data patterns about social support and mental wellbeing

claim: Universities should explore how they can facilitate work-related social support online for early-career researchers.
source: Universities should be exploring how they can facilitate work-related social support online.
evidence: Recommendation based on findings about social support and mental wellbeing

claim: More complex analyses are required to tease out the potential effect of gender and caregiving responsibilities on wellbeing of early-career researchers during lockdown.
source: More complex analyses are now required to also tease out the potential effect of gender and caregiving responsibilities on wellbeing.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitations and need for further analysis

claim: Around 60% of UK doctoral students and early-career researchers identified that their university had made arrangements for skills training to take place online during lockdown.
source: While around 60% of respondents identified that their university had made arrangements for skills training to take place online, more attention here may be beneficial, as our analysis indicates that access to online skills training is connected to better mental wellbeing.
evidence: Based on survey data about access to online skills training

claim: Access to online skills training is connected to better mental wellbeing among early-career researchers during lockdown.
source: While around 60% of respondents identified that their university had made arrangements for skills training to take place online, more attention here may be beneficial, as our analysis indicates that access to online skills training is connected to better mental wellbeing.
evidence: Based on analysis of survey data showing correlation between training access and wellbeing

claim: More attention to online skills training may be beneficial for early-career researchers during lockdown.
source: While around 60% of respondents identified that their university had made arrangements for skills training to take place online, more attention here may be beneficial, as our analysis indicates that access to online skills training is connected to better mental wellbeing.
evidence: Recommendation inferred from the connection between training and wellbeing

claim: There are links between levels of mental distress and support provided by supervisors or line managers during lockdown.
source: We also found links between levels of mental distress and support provided by supervisors or line managers.
evidence: Based on analysis of survey data examining relationship between supervisor support and mental distress

claim: Two-thirds of UK doctoral students and early-career researchers reported that they felt their supervisor or line manager had done all they could or should do to provide support during lockdown.
source: Two-thirds of respondents reported that they felt their supervisor or line manager had done all they could or should do to provide support at this time.
evidence: Based on survey responses about supervisor support

claim: Where strong supervisor or line manager support was identified, early-career researchers reported lower levels of mental distress during lockdown.
source: Where strong support was identified, respondents also reported lower levels of mental distress.
evidence: Based on analysis of survey data showing correlation between support and distress levels

claim: Supervisors and line managers have also been impacted by the lockdown.
source: It is vital to remember that the supervisors and line managers have also been impacted by the lockdown.
evidence: General knowledge about widespread lockdown impacts

claim: Many early-career researchers recognized and commented on the fact that supervisors have been impacted by lockdown, understanding gaps in support due to supervisors having children at home.
source: This is something that many respondents recognised and commented on — understanding, for example, that there may have been certain gaps in support because supervisors currently have children at home.
evidence: Based on qualitative comments from survey respondents

claim: Continued strong support from supervisors will help early-career researchers during lockdown.
source: However, continued strong support from supervisors will help early-career researchers.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between supervisor support and lower mental distress

claim: Around half of UK doctoral students and early-career researchers identified that their supervisor or line manager had made arrangements to support them to stay in touch with peers and colleagues at their university during lockdown.
source: Around half of respondents identified that their supervisor or line manager had made arrangements to support them to stay in touch with peers and colleagues at their university; these respondents also reported lower levels of loneliness.
evidence: Based on survey data about arrangements for peer contact

claim: Early-career researchers whose supervisors made arrangements to support staying in touch with peers reported lower levels of loneliness during lockdown.
source: Around half of respondents identified that their supervisor or line manager had made arrangements to support them to stay in touch with peers and colleagues at their university; these respondents also reported lower levels of loneliness.
evidence: Based on analysis of survey data showing correlation between peer contact arrangements and loneliness

claim: Online lab groups and virtual catch-ups can work effectively for researchers during lockdown.
source: Online lab groups and virtual catch-ups really can work.
evidence: Based on experience and observations of virtual research groups

claim: There are opportunities for digital connection with colleagues working around the world during lockdown.
source: Most researchers may be physically distant at present, but there are fantastic opportunities for digital connection, including with colleagues working around the world.
evidence: Based on knowledge of available digital communication technologies

claim: SMaRteN set up a virtual, weekly lab group for early-career researchers and doctoral students working on student mental health at the start of lockdown.
source: At the start of the lockdown SMaRteN set up a virtual, weekly lab group for early-career researchers and doctoral students working on student mental health (www.smarten.org.uk/lab-group).
evidence: Direct statement about an initiative undertaken by the organization

claim: The SMaRteN virtual lab group functions like any other lab group with guest speakers and paper discussions.
source: This is just like any other lab group – we have guest speakers and we discuss papers.
evidence: Description of the virtual lab group activities

claim: The SMaRteN virtual lab group has brought together researchers from all across the UK and from Australia.
source: The only exception is that we have been able to bring together researchers from all across the UK and recently, from Australia.
evidence: Direct statement about the geographic reach of the virtual lab group

claim: Universities should prioritize their doctoral and early-career researchers during the pandemic.
source: Universities should be prioritising their doctoral and early-career researchers, a population that is already in a precarious employment position, and whose members now face serious uncertainties around their future within academia.
evidence: Recommendation based on the documented precarious position and uncertainties

claim: Doctoral and early-career researchers are in a precarious employment position.
source: Universities should be prioritising their doctoral and early-career researchers, a population that is already in a precarious employment position, and whose members now face serious uncertainties around their future within academia.
evidence: Based on survey data about contracts, extensions, and employment uncertainty

claim: Doctoral and early-career researchers face serious uncertainties around their future within academia due to the pandemic.
source: Universities should be prioritising their doctoral and early-career researchers, a population that is already in a precarious employment position, and whose members now face serious uncertainties around their future within academia.
evidence: Based on survey data about concerns, contract endings, and lack of extensions

claim: Many early-career researchers have seen months or even years of work disrupted or destroyed by the rapid closure of laboratories.
source: Many have seen months or even years of work disrupted or destroyed by the rapid closure of laboratories; others have had fieldwork cancelled and face-to-face training opportunities curtailed.
evidence: Based on survey responses about research disruptions

claim: Some early-career researchers have had fieldwork cancelled and face-to-face training opportunities curtailed due to lockdown.
source: Many have seen months or even years of work disrupted or destroyed by the rapid closure of laboratories; others have had fieldwork cancelled and face-to-face training opportunities curtailed.
evidence: Based on survey responses about research disruptions

claim: Early-career researchers with children or other caring responsibilities are struggling with the reality that they cannot work while peers around them seem to be getting ahead.
source: Those with children or other caring responsibilities are struggling with the reality that they cannot work, while peers around them seem to be 'getting ahead'.
evidence: Based on survey responses or observations about caregiving impacts

claim: Universities and funders must take on some responsibility for helping early-career researchers cope with the disruptions to their work caused by the pandemic.
source: Universities and funders must take on some responsibility for helping this community cope with the disruptions to their work.
evidence: Normative recommendation based on documented disruptions and challenges

claim: Thousands of UK doctoral students and early-career researchers shared the repercussions of lockdown on their work and wellbeing.
source: Thousands of UK doctoral students and early-career researchers shared the repercussions of lockdown on their work and wellbeing.
evidence: Statement about the survey sample size and scope
